title: Counting the units
hook: two at dawn, four, four, three at sunset, four at night

segments.voice: Yesterday: taslim, the closing, right, then left. Your line was peace, both ways. Did you leave a room or a call with a word of peace? Day one hundred nine.

Some things you learn as a rhythm before you learn them as facts. The number of days in the months: thirty days has September. A phone number sung in an old commercial. The daily prayers can be learned the same way, as a string of numbers said in one breath: two, four, four, three, four. It sounds like a code. It's actually a map of the whole day. And each of those numbers counts one thing: a unit of the prayer. You've learned every piece of it this week. Today: how the pieces add up.
screen: `THIRTY DAYS HAS SEPTEMBER.` → `TWO, FOUR, FOUR, THREE, FOUR.` → `A MAP OF THE DAY.`

segments.voice: The unit is called a rak'ah, from the same root as ruku', the bow. One rak'ah is one full cycle: standing and reciting, the bow, rising, two prostrations with the sitting between. The pieces from this past week, in order, make one rak'ah. The daily prayers are built out of them. Fajr, at dawn: two. Dhuhr, midday: four. Asr, afternoon: four. Maghrib, sunset: three. Isha, night: four. Seventeen in all, every day. After every second rak'ah, the person sits for the tashahhud; in the last one, they add the taslim. So a four-rak'ah prayer has a sitting in the middle and one at the end. Why these numbers? The tradition keeps them because this is how the Prophet ﷺ prayed. But there is a story about them. Aisha, his wife, said in a hadith in Bukhari that the prayer was first made obligatory as two rak'ahs each. Then the traveler's prayer was left at two, and the prayer at home was increased. That's why, to this day, a traveler shortens the fours to two. The Qur'an gives the permission, in Surah an-Nisa: no sin in shortening the prayer on a journey. The dawn prayer stays two. The sunset prayer stays three. So the numbers carry a little history in them. Two was the original shape. The day's middle prayers grew. And on the road, the fours go back to the original two.
screen: `RAK'AH — ONE FULL CYCLE.` · `SEVENTEEN, EVERY DAY.` · `FIRST, TWO EACH.` · `ON THE ROAD, FOUR BECOMES TWO.` · then, large: `TWO, FOUR, FOUR, THREE, FOUR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: count on your fingers once. Hold up your hand. Thumb: fajr, two. Index finger: dhuhr, four. Middle finger: asr, four. Ring finger: maghrib, three. Little finger: isha, four. Say it through slowly, then say just the numbers, two, four, four, three, four. Then let your hand rest, and picture one whole rak'ah from standing to the second prostration, in your mind, slowly. If you pray, you know where you'll be at the next one. The bell holds the time.
Rak'ah. One unit of prayer, from standing to the second prostration; seventeen of them every day. Today's word.
Your line: two, four, four, three, four. Say it once at each meal today, and see if it sticks by tonight. Day one hundred nine.

howItsDone: Muslims pray seventeen obligatory rak'ahs a day: two at fajr, four at dhuhr, four at asr, three at maghrib and four at isha, and travelers commonly shorten the four-rak'ah prayers to two.

fork.setup: you're on a long journey and it's time for dhuhr, normally four rak'ahs. what does the tradition allow?
fork.reveal: a traveler shortens the four-rak'ah prayers to two; Aisha said the traveler's prayer was simply left at the original two.

original.note: Arabic: one unit of prayer, from the root of ruku', the bow.

trapdoor: what you thought: Muslims pray a certain number of times.
what it means: each prayer is built of rak'ahs, full cycles, seventeen a day in the pattern two, four, four, three, four.
what a scholar hears: Aisha's report that the prayer began as two (Bukhari 350), and qasr, shortening on a journey, from 4:101.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 350 (Aisha: the prayer first made obligatory as two rak'ahs)
Qur'an 4:101 (no sin in shortening the prayer on a journey)

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: hook no longer claims 'Muslim children often learn' the numbers this way; cut 'nobody gives a reason from logic' (scholars have discussed the wisdom of the numbers); fixed 'since day one hundred one' (the rak'ah's pieces run days 102–106); the last line no longer echoes day 111's 'the prayer fits you'.
Hadith number cited from memory; please confirm.

4:101 in its text mentions fear of attack; scholars (following a report from Umar, Muslim 686) apply shortening to all travel. The script paraphrases only 'no sin in shortening the prayer on a journey'.
Hanafis hold shortening is required for travelers, others that it's permitted; the fork's reveal says 'shortens' and 'allow'. Distance thresholds are not covered.
Seventeen counts obligatory rak'ahs only; sunnah prayers and witr are not mentioned.
